The next two statues of dancing Śiva to examine 
are from Lương Hậu village, Hương Thuỷ district 
of Huế city (Fig. 8.4 ), and from Phong Lệ, Đà Nẵng 
(Fig. 8.5); the main reason for grouping these two 
together is that both have sixteen arms and the 
arms are prominently depicted. In both of these 
sculptures, we do not see the members of Śiva’s 
family; instead, the emphasis is on his worshippers. 
The Śiva tympanum was discovered in Lương Hậu 
village and thus called Lương Hậu tympanum (Fig. 
8.4). This is the most recently discovered of the 
statues discussed here, as it was found a little over 
a decade ago. As far as I know, there are no publi-
cations on this sculpture in Western languages yet. 
The archeologist Lê Đình Phụng (2007 : 113–117 ) 
was the first scholar to publish information on this 
sculpture, which he dated to the 9 th to 10 th centu-
ries. However, the art historian Ngô Văn Doanh 
(2012 ) suggested that this dancing Śiva shares 
common characteristics with the 8th century Mỹ 
Sơn Śiva tympana A1 and C1 mentioned above 
and thus dated it to the 8th century. It was dis-
covered near the Bà Yàng shrine (the shrine of 
the ‘Heavenly Lady’), which is also known as Bà 
Chuẩn Đề (‘Lady of compassion, saviour, protector 
of Dharma’). After the discovery of this tympanum, 
local villagers brought it to the shrine and have 
worshipped it ever since as the main deity because 
they thought that she was the multi-armed Bud -
dhist bodhisattva Phật Bà Quan Âm (Guan-yin/
Avalokiteśvara). Śiva here has sixteen arms but 
holds no attributes at all; instead, the focus is on 
his hand gestures. Aside from his front right hand 
being in abhaya-mudrā (‘non-fear’ gesture) while 
his front left hand is in gajahasta-mudrā (‘ele-
phant hand’ gesture), all the right-hand gestures 
are symmetric with the left side. The two upper-
most hands seem to be holding something like a 
banded snake over his head. This is reminiscent 
of a 5 th century Gupta multi-armed Śiva dancing 
sculpture from Sirpur (see the image in Sivara-
mamurti 1974 : 172) whose topmost pair of hands 
holds up a snake while the two main front hands 
are in the gestures of abhaya-mudrā and gajahas-
ta-mudrā, the same as the Śiva from Lương Hậu. 
The only difference between the Indian’s Gupta 
dancing Śiva and the one from Lương Hậu lies in 
the attributes the Indian Śiva carries in other arms 
Fig. 8.4: Dancing Śiva, Shrine B à Y àng. H ương Thu ỷ, 
Huế. (Photo: 
Trần Kỳ Phương) 
such as the triśūla, ḍamaru, and kapāla. Indeed, it 
is from the Gupta period that representations of 
dancing Śiva in visual form became identifiable. In 
this Lương Hậu tympanum, Śiva is standing on a 
dwarf or the demon Apasmāra and, interestingly, 
the dwarf is looking straight at us. This is the only 
Cam representation of Śiva dancing on a dwarf 
that faces directly to the viewers. It is also very rare 
in India to have the dwarf placed in this position 
while supporting dancing Śiva. I was able to find 
only a few such cases, the first being the depiction 
of the 2 nd century BC–1 st century CE Gudimal -
lam liṅga (in southeastern Andhra Pradesh), which 
shows a merging of aniconic and anthropomorphic 
manifestations of Śiva, and the second being the 
9th-century CE Pallava bronze sculptures from 
Kuram, Nallur, and Kilakkadu in Tamil Nadu.21 
An Apasmāra under dancing Śiva’s foot is common 
in South Indian art, though the dwarf more often 
turns toward the left, and sometimes to the right, 
but rarely directly toward the viewers. Further-
more, in the Lương Hậu tympanum, there are two 
devoted worshippers, a male figure on Śiva’s right 
who looks more like a sage than an ordinary, and 
another male figure on his left who is most proba-
bly a devotee. None of Śiva’s family members nor 
his favourite attendant Bh ṛṅgin were depicted.

The dancing Śiva from Phong Lệ, Đà Nẵng  
(Fig. 8.5) is one of the best-carved and preserved 
Cam sculptures among all the depictions of dancing 
Śiva. There is a proportional balance between left  
and right and between the upper and lower parts 
of the sculpture. All the figures fit perfectly in the 
space of the arched form of the tympanum. The 
artist managed to bring out the overall harmony 
among all the figures in this sculpture in terms of 
the facial expressions of Śiva and his worshippers, 
and the techniques for proportional measurement 
of the statue. Śiva here is depicted with a crescent 
moon inserted in his headdress, one of his first 
identifying characteristics. Śiva has sixteen arms 
with all of the hands in identical gestures. Pierre 
Baptiste (2005: 237; 2018: 210–211) asserts that 
the hand gestures of the main arms, even though 
looking like vitarka-mudrā (hand gesture of argu-
mentation or discussion in which the tips of the 
thumb and the index finger touch while the other three fingers remain straight), are more likely the 
arālahasta (the hand gesture in which the index 
finger is bent and the thumb is held close to the 
palm, the tips do not necessary touch one another, 
and the three other fingers remain straight) de-
scribed in the dance manual Nāṭyaśāstra.22 In 
the upper part of the right main arm we see the 
serpent Śe ṣa that curls as his armband or bracelet 
ornament. There is a harpist and a drummer on 
each side of Śiva. There are also several floating

In researching Cam-Khmer interactions, Peter 
Sharrock (2018 : 111) stated that the period of the 
early 12th to early 13 th centuries saw ‘a succession 
of friendships, and military, economic and cul -
tural alliances.’ He explains that the Khmer King 
Sūryavarman II (1113 –1149  CE) helped the Cam to 
fight against Đại Việt to recover their lands during 
the 1120 s and that, after the Chinese Song empire 
opened up foreign trade by sea, the Cam and Khmer 
became closer allies by developing the Thị Nại port 
in Vijaya. This alliance can be seen in the growth in 
trade and the visible Khmer influence in architec-ture and statuary in southern Camp
ā. Particularly, 
Sharrock (ibid.: 116) suggests that the evidence of 
Khmer influence on Cam temple art and statuary 
can be seen in the Tháp Mẫm style, especially the 
high reliefs of dancers and the Garuḍa decorative 
motifs. The dancing Śiva from Tháp Mẫm also 
attests to Khmer influence in religious art, for in-
stance the detailed decorations of heavy jewellery. 
Actually, prior to the 10 th century, there is only a 
single anthropomorphic image of Śiva in any form 
in all of Khmer art (James 2011 : 199). However, 
from the 10 th to 13 th centuries, there were quite a 
number of tympana of Khmer dancing Śiva, such as 
those from Phnom Rung, Banteay Samre, Banteay 
Srei, Phnom Chisor, and Phimai.27 In Camp ā, no 
dancing Śiva has been dated to around the 11 th 
century; they appeared only in the 12 th to 13 th 
centuries, when the southern Cam of Vijaya were 
in close contact with the Khmer.

conclusion 
Dancing Śiva was visualized and iconographically 
represented in Camp ā as early as the 8th century 
and continued to hold an important place in Cam 
religious art up until the 13 th century. Interesting-
ly, the dancing Śiva dated between the 8th and 10 th 
centuries were all found in the northern regions 
of Campā (Indrapura, Amar āvatī), while the 
sculptures from the later period, between the 12 th 
to 13th centuries, came mainly from the southern 
part (Vijaya, and P āṇḍuraṅga), except the dancing 
Śiva from Mỹ Sơn H1 , which is a special case (it 
was found in Mỹ Sơn but bears strong similarities 
with the Tháp Mẫm decorative art style). Dancing 
Śivas found in the North were portrayed very often 
with his family members such as Pārvat ī, Gaṇeśa 
and Skanda, as well as with his attendants Bhṛ ṅgin, 
Nandin, and the dwarf Apasmāra. These charac -
ters were adopted directly from Indian iconogra-
phy. In addition, the crossed arms position and 
the dancing poses seem to be influenced by Indian 
Śaiva iconography of dancing Śiva. However, in 
the statues of dancing Śiva from the South, we do 
not see the portrayal of Śiva’s family members nor 
his attendants Bhṛ ṅgin, Nandin, and the dwarf 
Apasmāra. Instead, attributes of Śiva such as the 
trident (śūla or triśūla), a club (khaṭvā ṅga), a 
rosary, and an axe were depicted. These attributes 
were not main features of the 8th to 10 th centu-
ries sculptures found in the northern regions of 
Campā even though they had Indian antecedents. 
It is clear that the Cam selectively appropriated a 
number of Śaiva religious art features from various 
sources. One can ask why the northern Cam were 
not interested in those attributes of Śiva that were 
of the utmost importance. Śaivism was clearly a dominant religion of various Cam polities, but on 
the basis of this preliminary survey of the dancing 
Śiva iconographical representation it seems rea -
sonable to suggest that perhaps the form of Śaivism 
that was practiced in the northern part of Camp ā 
could have undergone modifications in the South-
ern part. After all, Camp ā never existed as a single 
entity and thus different varieties of Śaivism could 
have been practised more or less independently in 
different parts of Camp ā. 
For the time being, it is important to note that 
dancing Śiva was not a common element within 
Khmer religious art prior to the 10 th century and 
in fact there was only a single Khmer anthropo-
morphic image of Śiva in any form prior to the 
9th century. In insular Southeast Asia, images 
of dancing Śiva were not adopted and the only 
example of a dancing deity tentatively identified as 
Śiva can be seen is the dancing figures on the walls 
of Candi Śiva at the Prambanan temple complex 
in Central Java, dating from the 9 th century, but 
this is still a hypothesis and needs further research 
before it can be definitely confirmed (Iyer 1998 ). 
Thus, the 8th-century dancing Śiva tympana from 
Camp ā, of Lương Hậu, and Mỹ Sơn (A1 and C1
) 
may be regarded as the earliest depictions of the 
dancing Śiva in Southeast Asia. In the light of this 
fact, I suggest that Camp ā might have received a 
direct early transmission of religious art from India 
to its northern regions. Furthermore, on account of 
the close political and trading connections between 
southern Camp ā and the Khmer kings in the 12 th 
to 13th centuries, and of the elements of Khmer 
decorative motifs seen in dancing Śiva from Tháp 
Mẫm and Po Klaong Girai, I would suggest that 
Camp ā might have also received Khmer art influ-
ence during this period. In short, at this stage it is 
possible to speculate that in the early period, from 
the 8 th to 10 th centuries, Northern Camp ā seems 
to be influenced by Indian iconography through 
a direct transmission while from the 12th century 
onwards the presence of Khmer religious art influ-
ences and connections can be seen in the Cam art of Vijaya and P
āṇḍuraṅga. 
What is important to stress here is that the 
Cam did not simply copy and reproduce the reli-
gious art elements they received from Indian and 
Khmer sources, but rather adapted them and ex -
08_CreSouthV1_5P_28Jan22.indd   301 28/1/22   7:44 PM

--- [Page 304] ---
Mai Bùi Diệu Linh302
pressed new forms based on their own concepts. 
For instance, the uppermost hands interlocked 
and joined above Śiva’s head are a feature unique 
to southern Camp ā, which is especially strongly 
present in Cam art from the 12 th century in Vijaya 
and P āṇḍuraṅga, even though the exact meaning of 
this hand gesture as intended by the Cam remains 
unclear. The extant sculptures of dancing Śiva 
from Indrapura and Amar āvatī in the north of 
Camp ā did not employ this type of hand gesture, 
nor can this element be found in the religious art 
of Southeast Asia outside of Camp ā, thereby sug-
gesting a local interest. In addition, most of the 
Cam statues of dancing Śiva were depicted in the 
form of tympana that were intended to be placed 
at the main entrances of temples. This is the second 
most prominent position in a temple, second only 
to the central sanctuary icon. To have a dancing 
Śiva placed above the main entrance signifies that 
the temple belongs to Śiva as the central deity. Śiva 
has many manifestations and the fact that this man -
ifestation was selected to be represented on the 
tympanum suggests that the Cam were especially 
attracted to this form of Śiva.

introduction
The polities of Campā along the coast of 
central Vietnam were not politically united, 
but the Cams appear to have participat -
ed in temple and courtly culture, as can be seen 
through their inscriptions and image making. A 
16th-century Spanish account of the customs in 
Campā mentions at least five courtly festivals held 
annually by the Cam king, including feasts, plays, 
public races, and celebrations of elephant and tiger 
hunts (Souza and Turley 2016 : 677–680 ). In addi -
tion, Chinese histories describe the Cam kings per -
forming public processions with elephants, parasols, 
drums, and conches. These observations indicate 
a public display suggesting that the Cam polities 
shared political and cultural expression of power 
and religion.2 This chapter explores the extent to 
which the Cams incorporated themselves into the 
international political and economic sphere in the 
9th–10 th centuries by projecting onto their artistic 
1. I am indebted to research carried out by the late Julie 
Romain in her 2015 dissertation, ‘Courtly Culture and 
Visual Art in India: Rāmāyaṇa  Reliefs on Hindu Temples 
of the Sixth to Eighth Century’. She also offered advice and 
encouragement from the first time I met her in 2011 and 
throughout my graduate studies at UCLA in 2012–2017. In 
her dissertation, she argues that the R āmāyaṇa  rel iefs in 
Hindu temples reflected ‘secular, courtly culture’, and that 
the images of Rāma emphasize an honorific function, and 
highlight his role as a courtly hero. I thank Robert L. Brown, 
Peter Sharrock, and Andrea Acri for their comments on 
earlier versions of this chapter. In addition, two anony -
mous peer reviewers also provided helpful suggestions for 
revision.
2. Cefu yu
angui , 959.11288; Taiping yulan (Encyclopedia 
Assembled for Imperial Inspection during the Taiping Era) 
(983; Taibei: Shangwu yinshuguan, 1980), 786.3611.productions a complex and creative military and 
courtly culture. 
One of the most well-known sacred epics in 
South and Southeast Asia is the Rāmāyaṇa, the life 
story of Rāma, an avatar of Viṣṇu. Using textual 
sources, visual evidence, and recent scholarship, 
this chapter analyses the colossal Trà Kiệu pedestal 
within the context of the Rāmāyaṇa in Khmer and 
Javanese cultures during the 9th–10 th centuries. 
Visual evidence includes the Rāmāyaṇa sandstone 
reliefs preserved at the Đà Nẵng Museum of Cam 
Sculpture and imagery from three central Vietnam 
archaeological sites: Khương Mỹ, Chiên Đàn, and 
Chánh Lộ. The visual evidence shows three shared 
iconographic elements: archers with bows, archi -
tectural features, and dancing apsaras es found in 
Campā, East Java, and Cambodia. I suggest that 
the Rāmāyaṇa reliefs reveal that the Trà Kiệu 
pedestal found in a temple context also promoted 
courtly culture with close relationships to the art 
and cultures of Cambodia, East Java, and China in 
the 9th–10 th centuries. I define courtly culture as 
comprising ceremonial, celebratory, and martial 
activities with an emphasis on symbols of power, 
hierarchy, and etiquette for political motivations. 
Within the sacred sphere, the stone Trà Kiệu ped-
estal also commemorates royal-divine interactions 
through the narrative of the Rāmāyaṇa.3

has political implications as well. The royal court was also

history of the trà kiệu pedestal
The colossal Trà Kiệu pedestal and the liṅga-yoni  
were discovered in the 19 th century in Trà Kiệu 
village of Quảng Nam province in central Vietnam. 
The objects probably originated from point B 
in Trà Kiệu beside the main sanctuary, but not 
having been scientifically excavated, the original 
archaeological context of the pieces is unknown 
(Fig. 9.1).4 Early photographs of the Trà Kiệu ped-
estal suggest that it was once topped by a liṅga  
and thus focused on the worship of Śiva, but it is

of devotion. The first images of the Trà Kiệu ped-

Charles Lemire in an excursion report to Tourane, 
now modern-day Đà Nẵng, Vietnam. We do not 
know what sculptures were originally placed on 
the pedestal. During the colonial period, several 
different icons were displayed on the pedestal due 
to archaeological and curatorial considerations.5

5. Regardless of the reasons behind the arrangement, local

The Colossal Trà Kiệu Pedestal in Campā309
oral tradition that used various Indic heroes to tell 
local stories. The reliefs display what to modern 
audiences would seem a disjointed series of ex-
cerpts from epic or sacred narratives, but were 
likely well understood by the Cams through their 
own cultural lens. 
James Scott argues that ‘in the case of oral 
histories and narratives, the concept of “the orig-
inal” simply does not make sense. Oral culture 
exists and is sustained only through each unique 
performance at a particular time and place for an 
interested audience’ (Scott 2009 : 230). Seen from 
this perspective, the difficulty in locating the orig-
inal or a single story for the carvings on the Trà 
Kiệu pedestal is not surprising. The recourse to 
Indian texts to comprehend Southeast Asian art is 
found in most scholarly interpretations, but how 
those texts were understood in Southeast Asia 
is not certain. Even if there was some certainty 
about the identification of a group of characters 
in terms of a specific text, we cannot know if the 
local interpretation was consistent with the Indic 
textual one. As far as I know, there are no extant 
Cam representations of the Kauṇḍinya myth or 
life scenes of Kṛṣṇa and the visual representations 
depicted on the Trà Kiệu pedestal would be unique 
if we identify them as such. Based on inscriptions 
and other visual arts related to the Rāmāyaṇa in 
Campā, there is sufficient visual evidence that the 
Trà Kiệu pedestal depicts characters from the 
Rāmāyaṇa, but which specific stories and scenes 
from the epic remains subject to debate.
In addition to conflicting interpretations 
about the story carved on the Trà Kiệu pedestal, 
the scholarship is not conclusive about its date. 
Two time periods are proposed in the literature 
for the object: early 7 th-century or a much later 
one, closer to the 10 th century. For instance, Henri 
Parmentier and Trầ n Kỳ Phương date the pedes-
tal to the 7 th–8 th century, while Jean Boisselier, 
Emmanuel Guillon, and Anne-Valérie Schweyer 
place the pedestal in the 10 th century. Using recent 
scholarship, archaeological findings, and careful 
visual analysis, I will argue that the Trà Kiệu ped-
estal dates closest to the 10 th century. dating of the liṅga-yoni and the  
trà kiệu pedestal
It is possible that the large liṅga-yoni still paired 
with the Trà Kiệu pedestal in the Đà Nẵng Museum 
of Cam Sculpture is dated earlier than the pedestal 
itself. Trần Kỳ Phương argues that a 7th-century 
yoni from Hà Trung is similar to the form of the liṅ -
ga-yoni on top of the Trà Kiệu pedestal (Trần 2018 : 
128). The Hà Trung yoni is elaborately decorated 
with two rows of petals. The first row includes four-
leaf petals with an inverted fleuron at the centre. On 
the bottom of the Hà Trung yoni , there are addi -
tional carvings of floral, leaf, and spiral decorations. 
The petals are separated between another inverted 
fleuron carved on the top rim. This fleuron motif 
also appears on the Trà Kiệu pedestal. 
A second, round yoni with the inscription of 
Prakāśadharma (C. 97) from Mỹ Sơn is also com-
parable stylistically to the liṅga-yoni of Trà Kiệu 
(Trần 2018: 128). The yoni is carved with an in -
scription on the centre of its body, which dates to 
the 7th century (Fig. 9.4). The inscription states, 
‘this [kośa] for [the liṅga of] Vāmeśvara, installed 
by Sri Vikrāntavarman, the lion among kings, will 
endure as long as the world exists’ (Golzio 2004: 
29). The kośa is a metal cover for the liṅga that 
can be added and removed, and is thought to be 
installed as an offering after lustration rituals (Guy 
1998, 2018: 89). This suggests that various things 
were placed on liṅgas and the placement of objects 
could also change over time.8 Except for stylistic 
connections, there is little evidence that the inscrip -
tion of Prakāśadharma is related to the Trà Kiệu 
pedestal and the liṅga-yoni. The base of the yoni 
with inscription carries decorative designs of lotus 
petals, with one large single petal alternating with 
two doubled petals around the rim. Trần argues 
that the ‘round-shaped yoni decorated with large 
doubled lotus petals was introduced as a new art 
form in the late seventh century’ (Trần 2018: 128).

Liṅga-yonis were constructed in different shapes 
and sizes with varying decorative motifs from the 
7th to the 9 th centuries. There is a circular hole 
in the yoni and the museum has recently inserted 
what it sees as the correct Trà Kiệu liṅga. However, 
the hole does not descend into the square base. 
Without the liṅga-yoni, the base is an autonomous 
object, and there is no other Cam yoni with images 
from the Rāmāyaṇa. 
On the basis of the above considerations, I 
suggest the pedestal should be studied separately 
from the liṅga-yoni, without excluding the possi -
bility that another deity or multiple objects may 
be originally paired with the decorated base. A 
9th–10 th-century date is the most likely as the 
subject and decoration of the reliefs can be com -
pared to prominent 10 th-century artworks related 
to the Rāmāyaṇa in Java, Cambodia, and Campā.9

Levin sees architectural connections between 
Cam and Javanese temples. She states, ‘the assigna -
tion of Khương Mỹ to the early Classical phase of 
[Cam] art [10 th century] was made on the overall 
basis of architectural ornamentation and particu-
lar stylistic links shared with Classical Javanese 
monuments’ (Levin 2008 : 90). She also observes 
an association between Campā’s matrilineal society 
and Sītā depicted as a powerful figure, rejecting 
Rāvaṇa’s advances, at Khương Mỹ. Her observa -

bolstered by Tr ần Kỳ Phương and Rie Nakamura’s 
article about the dualist cult of Cam society. They 
suggest that two sanctuaries, M ỹ Sơn and Pô Nagar, 
‘reflect certain characteristics of the cosmological 
dualism’ defined as a Cam male and female dichot -
omy (Trần and Nakamura 2012 : 208 ).
Inscriptions and icons found at two Cam sites 
suggest that from the 8th to the 13th century, M ỹ 
Sơn was built for the God Bhadreśvara (benev-
olent Śiva/Mountain/Father) and Pô Nagar for  
the Goddess Bhagavatī (Pô Nagar/Sea/Mother) 
(ibid.: 274). The authors conclude that M ỹ Sơn and 
Pô Nagar symbolized the female and male realm, 
respectively, thus revealing an emphasis on Cam 
cosmological dualism. In volume two of this edited 
collection, Roy E. Jordaan discusses the possibility 
for the representation of Sītā as Rāvaṇa’s daughter 
at Candi Prambanan. What is clear is that both 
cultures in Java and Campā had local expressions 
and an emphasis on lineage, kinship, and parent-
age, all of which reflect Southeast Asian traditions 
practised in the 9th–10th centuries. In addition,

Levin has theorized some connections of artistic 
elements such as temple motifs and foliage found 
in Campā and Java, which may have a common 
origin in China (Tu 2018 : 84). Following these 
suggestions, the artistic relationships to consider 
between Campā and related cultures would include 
Cambodia and China, as well as Java.
inscriptions and historical records
The interaction between Campā and Java is men -
tioned in inscriptions, which record, for example, 
Java’s sea attack against the Cams in the 8th century. 
An inscription dated to 787 /788  CE reads, 
Then owing to the excess of faults in the Kali 
Age it (i.e., the temple […]) was burnt by the 
army of Java coming by means of ships, and be -
came empty, in the year of the Śakas denoted 
‘nine, ambara, adri’ [709]. (Golzio 2004: 43)
Peter Sharrock has noted that the relationship 
between the Cams and the Khmers has ‘too often 
been characterized as continuous warfare. A close 
look shows a succession of friendships, and mili -
tary, economic and cultural alliances’ (Sharrock et 
al. 2018 : 111). Similar to the interaction between 
Campā and Cambodia, there is little detailed 
history of the nature and dating of the relationships 
between the Cams and the Javanese. However, there 
is evidence of contact, both military and economic. 
Arlo Griffiths states that ‘the ancient name 
of the island of Java, and its identifiability with 
various similar-sounding names known from 
ancient Southeast Asian, Chinese and Arab sources, 
is an old problem, compounded by the fact that 
similar-sounding and obviously related names in 
some modern mainland Southeast Asian languages 
refer not to the Javanese or to Java in particular, 
but to Malays or the Malay world in general, or to 
localities in northern Laos’ (Griffiths 2013 : 49). He 
suggests that Khmer inscriptions refer to the island 
of Java. Griffiths concludes that there were ‘inter-
national political relations between Khmer, Cam 
and Javanese polities in the late 8th and early 9th 
century of our era’ (ibid.: 76). The visual and textual 
evidence has not been comprehensively analysed, 
but both type of sources will shed some light on 
the warfare exchanges between the Cams and the Javanese, as well as less explored areas such as sim-
ilarities between their military and courtly cultures. 
Intriguing evidence for peaceful diplomatic in-
terchange is found in the 10 th-century Nhan Bièu 
inscription from Campā that records the historical 
connection between Java and Campā in the form 
of a royal officer’s two expeditions to Java. The in-
scription states, 
He was a favorite captain of the king Śrī Jaya- 
siṃhavarman and had riches equal to his de -
sires. He was named Pov Kluñ Piliḥ Rājadvāra. 
At the command of the king he went to the cap -
ital of Yavadvīpa on a diplomatic mission and 
obtained credit by the success of his under -
taking… Again, at the commands of the king 
he went to Yavadvīpa a second time and was 
successful in his undertaking. (Golzio 2004: 
112–113)
While we do not know the journey’s objectives, they 
were considered successful, and it is assumed that 
they would have introduced new cultural and re -
ligious knowledge to both the Javanese and Cam 
courts.
Chinese historical records indicate that the 
Cams exchanged Javanese textiles with China. For 
example, textual sources document that in 963  CE, 
an envoy from Campā brought to China differ -
ent types of Javanese textiles such as ‘gu  thin silk 
from the country of Ma-li-yan-luan in Java’ , and 
‘gu thin silk from Sha-wan in Java’ (Wade 2011 : 
161). Whether or not these were actual Javanese 
textiles cannot be verified, but what is important 
to stress is that the Chinese accepted the textiles as 
Javanese. The documents indicated that the Cams, 
the Chinese, and the Javanese operated within the 
international circle, either directly or indirectly 
during the 9th–10 th centuries. The Cams pre -
sented the Chinese with Javanese textiles, among 
other trade objects, while likely receiving military 
weapons and horses in exchange.11

to China in A Record of Buddhist Kingdoms (399 –
414 CE) indicated travels to Java-dvīpa (Java). His 
passage reads,

While Faxian’s stay in Java was due to a storm 
that drove his ship off course, Java and Sumatra 
became major destinations for Chinese monks in 
the 6th and 7 th centuries to stop en route on their 
voyages to India and study Buddhist texts and learn 
Sanskrit. The doors were open wide for cultural 
interchange.
Furthermore, Campā and Java are connected 
through their cultural appreciation and shared 
artistic iconography for the sacred epic, the 
Rāmāyaṇa. The visual and textual material in the 
Rāmāyaṇa reinforces kingship and ‘the develop -
ment of the notions of political authority in South -
east Asia, most notably in the ancient—and emi-
nently “Southeast Asian”—conception of the king 
as a “man of prowess” endowed with superhuman 
abilities and worshipped by his entourage in terms 
of bhakti relationships’ (Acri 2017 : 10). There is 
ample evidence that the R āmāyaṇa was celebrated 
in Campā. A Cam inscription dating to the 7th 
century reveals the worship and divine nature of 
Vālmīki, the mythical author of the R āmāyaṇa. 
The inscription reads,
The king Prakāśadharma, destroyer of all 
hordes of enemies, possessing the qualities of 
wisdom, power, patience, fortune, glory and 
firmness, desired in the world, after the enemy 
having vanished in autumn (?), accomplished 
here the place of veneration for the best of po -
ets and great Ṛṣi Vālmīki whom he honored 
full of sorrow with the Brahma-Śloka, he, who 
is the human form of the old male Viṣṇu… his temple… was built again. (Golzio 2004: 12)
In the inscription, the poet Vālmīki is honoured as 
a sage and an embodiment of Viṣṇu. In another inscription, the Mỹ Sơn Stele Inscrip -
tion of Prakāśadharma, dating to 656  CE, the king 
describes himself as
Constantly devoted to the Brāhmaṇas, the 
gods among men, (he was) gracefully attended 
by enemies subdued by his own prowess; (he 
was) the cause of Lakṣmī pride; Śrī Lakṣmī, 
in the fond hope that he was Rāma, son of 
king Daśaratha, dutifully followed him, and 
this was very worthy of her indeed! (Golzio  
2004: 20)
Here, the inscription places the Cam king on the 
same level as Rāma from the Rāmāyaṇa. The posi-
tion of king was often seized by usurpers through 
military prowess. Thus, the heroic Rāma, who was 
able to defeat all his enemies and rivals, was an ideal 
role model in Cam society. The kings often wrote 
of the ideal leader, frequently invoking the quintes-
sential heroic prince, Rāma. A 12 th-century Khmer 
inscription compares the Cam king to Rāvaṇa, the 
defeated enemy of Rāma. The inscription reads, 
‘Sri Jaya Indravarman, king of [Campā], arrogant 
as Rāvaṇa… having an army led by chariots, went 
to the country of Kambu equal to the heavens in 
order to fight’ (Thompson 2016 : 130). Both Khmer 
and Cam inscriptions indicate that the R āmāyaṇa 
was we
ll known by the 7 th century and continued 
to be mentioned in later inscriptions. 
military and temple culture 
Besides textual evidence, the Trà Kiệu pedestal is 
contemporary to 9th–10 th-century artistic vestiges 
from Campā that promote military culture. Mili -
tary culture includes organized labour of people for 
martial activites such as battles and horse-riding 
to express notions of political power and domi -
nance. Scholars indicate that the horse carved in 
high relief on the Trà Kiệu pedestal is stylistically 
similar to the two horses on a 10 th-century relief 
showing two polo players (Fig. 9.5). Polo games are 
connected to military training since they endow 
players with ‘speed, skill, stamina, and bravery’ 
(Bower and Mackenzie 2004 : 283). The necklace 
with round bells around the horse, hanging from 
the collar is similar in both reliefs. Furthermore, the

horse hoof is rendered in the same realistic style. 
Another similarity includes the polo player’s hairdo 
with a large, round bun tied behind the head, which 
echoes the hair of the figures illustrated on the Trà 
Kiệu pedestal (Fig. 9.3 ). This is the only surviving 
example of polo playing depicted in Southeast 
Asian art. Polo games are commonly associated 
with the horse-riding cultures of the Asian steppes, 
a region with few trees, forests, and large areas of 
open space, but were also popular in Tang China 
(Nguyễn 2018 : 206–209 ). The Cams were also ac -
complished horsemen and even reached Angkor 
by horse-drawn chariots in 1177  CE (Thompson 
2016 : 6).12 The image of two polo players on the 
balustrade of a Cam temple informs viewers about 
its significance in elite culture, specifically the royal 
court, emphasizing some traits of Sinitic courtly 
culture in Campā.

Most representations depict Rāvaṇa shaking the 
mountain placed at the bottom under the enor -
mous Śiva temple that is rock cut into the moun-
tain. The mountain itself is a metaphor for the 
home of Śiva and Pārvatī. In addition, the temple 
itself symbolized the sacred mountain that is the 
home of a gods, a pīṭha. At the rock-cut Kailāsa 
Temple at Ellora in India, Rāvaṇa is depicted at 
the base of the temple where he is carved into a 
deep cavity (Dhar 2019 : 364). The temple is liter-
ally carved out of the mountain itself, so that the 
mountain and temple are one. Rāvaṇa is placed as 
if under the temple, trying to shake it, indicating 
its identification as Mount Kailāsa on which Śiva 
and Pārvatī live. The temple is the mountain on 
which Śiva and all of the gods live, thus a pīṭha. 
The gods can also descend from the metaphorical 
mountain to the physical Cam temple, the seat 
of the divine. Therefore, the figure from Đồ ng 
Dương is a symbol of the nature of the pedestal 
and the sacred pīṭha, not of any specific narrative. 
Pierre Baptiste has discussed the importance of the  
pīṭha in Śilpaś āstra texts (Baptiste 2005 : 109). This  
also indicates that various gods and their home—
whether they were Buddhist, Hindu, or stemming 
from local beliefs—were integrated and revered in 
the highly developed Cam temple culture during the 9th–10 th centuries. 
The identity of the carved figure on the Đồ ng 
Dương block remains unknown, but Parul Pandya 
Dhar argues that ‘what is certain, however, is the 
deliberate adaptation of a well-known Śaivite 
iconographic formula, namely the Rāvaṇānu -
grahamūrti, at the predominately Buddhist site 
of Đồ ng Dương’ (Dhar 2019 : 372). The figure’s 
iconographical features with the attributes of 
Rāvaṇa attests to the popularity of the R āmāyaṇa  
during the 9 th–10 th centuries in Cam Buddhist or 
Hindu contexts. These features include the multi-
ple heads and arms, and the body tilted back with 
legs bent, which create energy and movement in 
the Cam relief.16 With eight arms spread out, the

the Khmer king’s actual throne looked like, the 
sacred power of the pedestal is connected to both 
the divine and the royal spheres.

archers with bows
The iconography of the archer with bow is essential 
for the identification of the figure on the Trà Kiệu 
pedestal as Rāma (Fig. 9.8). The frontal Rāma is 
shown as an archer who lunges, with his left leg 
slightly bent and extended forward and right leg 
bent at the knee, a pose known as praty ālīḍhāsa-
na.19 In his left hand, he holds his bow, while his 
right arm is pulled back to launch the arrow. In the 
narrative, King Janaka agrees to give his daughter 
Sītā as wife to anyone who can bend his sacred bow. 
Rāma not only bends the bow, but breaks it in front 
of the king and his court. Depicted on the Trà Kiệu 
pedestal, Rāma’s broken bow is bent on the top, 
revealing his physical strength. Furthermore, Rāma 
is also carved in a similar position in a 9th-century 
Javanese relief in the Prambanan temple, showing 
Rāma who defeats various creatures at sea (Fig. 9.9). 
Characters in poses resembling praty ālīḍhāsana 
also appear in other 10th-century artistic vestiges 
of Campā. Extant examples of this posture include 
two male figures wrestling each other. The two op-
ponents place their hands on each partner’s thigh 
with arm raised, carved in high relief on the stair-
19. Robert L. Brown, personal communication, 2015.case of the 10th-century Khương Mỹ temple (Fig. 
9.10). In a second example, a 10 th-century relief 
also illustrates two defeated figures and a stand -
ing monkey with an inscription that reads, ‘army 
of monkeys in the middle of the city of Laṅkā... 
hurling’ (Griffiths et al. 2012 : 238) (Fig. 9.11). With 
its teeth exposed, the monkey stands in a similar 
position to Rāma and the two wrestlers, a posture 
that indicates physical strength and stamina. 
The image of the archer in praty ālīḍhāsana 
with the iconography of the arched bow is shared 
between Javanese and Cam artistic conventions. 
In 2001 , archaeologists found sculptural reliefs 
depicting the major events from the R āmāyaṇa at 
the foundation of the Khương Mỹ temple. Scholars 
have found captions on the foundation bases, but 
most of them are illegible. One, written in Cam, 
mentions characters from the R āmāyaṇa such as 
Lakṣmaṇa and Śūrpaṇakhā (ibid.: 23
9). The Cam 
language contains words borrowed from San-
skrit and the inscription is written in the same 
style found in two bas-reliefs held at the Đà Nẵng 
Museum of Cham Sculpture. Thus, scholars have 
suggested that the reliefs from Khương Mỹ and 
the two R āmāyaṇa bas-reliefs are dateable to the 
10th century (ibid.). A foundation base at Khương 
Mỹ depicts Rāma shooting an arched arrow from 
his bow to capture the golden deer (Levin 2008 : 
87). The deer stands in front of a large tree with its 
body pierced by the arrow. The position of the bow 
with his left hand and the rendering of the bow in 
profile echoes the image of Rāma holding Rudra’s 
bow on the Trà Kiệu pedestal (Fig. 9.8 ). 
The movement of artistic motifs across geo -
graphical and cultural boundaries was often docu-
mented in terms of decorative objects. Metal dishes 
travelled easily across borders due to their diminu-tive size and to their lack of esoteric iconographic 
and religious meanings. One example is a 9th-cen-
tury imported dish found in Campā, which illus -
trates three mounted horse riders holding either a 
spear or an arched bow, alternating between ele -
phants and trees (Fig. 9.12 ). The mounted archer 
with bow shoots an animal leaping from behind a 
tree. The archer is depicted in a manner similar to the one seen on the foundation bases at Khương 
Mỹ, and also resonates with the iconography of 
Rāma’s bow on the Trà Kiệu pedestal (Fig. 9.8 ).

The bow is carved in the same way as in the dish 
and the relief at Khương Mỹ, showing the arch of 
the bow slightly bent on the edges with the archer’s 
hand firmly gripping the centre of the bow. A relief 
from Candi Panataran (12 th–15 th century) in East 
Java depicts Indrajit, the son of Rāvaṇa, attacking 
Hanumān with a bow, reflecting the same iconog-
raphy of the mounted archer with bow (Fig. 9.13 ). 
The sculptor highlights a thick bow arched on the 
ends similar to a flying boomerang. I suggest that 
the archer with bow is a visual representation of 
the king’s perceived military stability in Campā 
and Java. Even more generally, the archer with a 
bow exemplifies the male hero, both human and 
deity, as a symbol of power, bravery, and victory. 
architectural features
The image of the open-air pavilion on the Khương 
Mỹ relief reveals a continuing shared Cam-Khmer 
artistic tradition. The roof of the Cam pavilion 
includes pointed crenellations, a motif first seen 
in the 7 th century at Wat Eng Khna. The Khmer 
lintel shows the Lingodbhavamūrti myth and the 
consecration of a king seated in an open-air pa-
vilion with similar crenellations (Guy 2014 : 165) 
(Fig. 9.14). Khmer examples with extant pointed 
roof crenellations include the 11 th-century temple 
of Preah Vihear and 12 th-century reliefs from 
Banteay Chhmar. While seen in the Khmer lintel, 
such crenellations have not been found on Cam 
temples. The Cam reliefs express an emphasis on 
martial symbols, as the crenellations reflected a de-
fensive wall to launch arrows similar to the carved 
imagery of Rāma’s arrows. Cecelia Levin suggests 
that the open pavilion has Javanese, Chinese, and 
Malay architectural links, but another possibility is 
that this stems from a local Cam-Khmer creation 
(Levin 2008 : 99). I interpret the crenellations as 
an artistic convention shared between the Khmer 
and Cam, reflecting similarities in military culture. 
Iconographical analysis beyond the region of 
Campā connects its art production to Cambodia 
and Java during the 9th–10 th centuries. An icono-
graphic feature on the Trà Kiệu pedestal is the 
fleuron hanging from the upper border above the 
kneeling female (Fig. 9.15 ). Rather than being used 
as a decorative border as in Khmer lintels, the motif is used instead to mark the central character in the 
Trà Kiệu relief panel. Martin Polkinghorne (2007 : 
226) identified the inverted fleuron as a common 
motif found on Khmer temple lintels and repre -
sentative of a 10 th-century workshop in Cambodia 
(Fig. 9.16). The inclusion of the motif suggests a 
shared artistry between Cambodia and Campā in 
the 10 th century.
Another feature linking the Javanese and the 
Cams is the representation of a miniature temple, 
accompanied by an active figure. This highlights 
the importance of temple culture and documents that religious activity was carried out both inside 
and around the temple. As mentioned earlier, an 
example of this is a 10 th-century lintel from Mỹ Sơn 
F1, which depicts Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa 
(Fig. 9.17). In praty ālīḍhāsana
 and other positions, 
the multi-headed and twenty-armed Rāvaṇa is ren -
dered beside a miniature temple. A Javanese relief 
from the R āmāyaṇa at Candi
 Panataran shows a 
temple reminiscent to the carved miniature temple 
found in Mỹ Sơn F1 (Fig. 9.18 ). The representation 
of a temple with an active figure such as Rāvaṇa and 
the actual temple relief links temple culture with 
people. The illustration of the miniature temple 
reflects Javanese temples such as the smaller dated 
temple in the Panataran complex.20

and Southeast Asia, and there is some specific 
iconography to the apsarases in Cambodia, Java, 
and Campā. One of the four sides of the Trà Kiệu 
pedestal depicts a row of eleven dancing apsarases 
(Fig. 9.3).21 In the relief, the dancers’ two legs are

While Pierre Baptiste does not focus on the nar -
rative reliefs of the colossal Trà Kiệu pedestal, he 
makes the distinction between a pedestal and the 
foundation base of Cam temples. Baptiste argues 
that another object found in Trà Kiệu, the so-called 
‘dancer’ pedestal is not a pedestal, but rather the 
decorated high-relief foundation of the Trà Kiệu 
tower. This relief is by art historical consensus con-
temporary with the Trà Kiệu pedestal. The dancer’s 
head is tilted with one hand close to her head, while 
she softly twists and curves her upper body and legs 
in the relief, reflecting the super-human abilities 
of the female. 
The later, 11 th-century sandstone bas-reliefs on 
the foundation walls of three Chiên Đàn temples 
(Fig. 9.19) reveal close similarities to the narrative 
reliefs of Trà Kiệu. The architects of the Chiên 
Đàn temples may have copied the images from 
the Trà Kiệu pedestal (Schweyer and Paisarn 
2012 : 145). The dancing figures resemble Cam and 
Khmer lintels, representing Śiva dancing on an al-
tar-pedestal in this position. In Java, the 9 th-centu -
ry Candi Prambanan also depicts reliefs of female 
dancers to evoke the spiritual realm (Fig. 9.21 ). 
The foundation reliefs of the Chiên Đàn towers 
of Campā depict dancers with the same dance 
position, resonating with the scene from the Trà 
Kiệu pedestal (Fig. 9.22 ). The images on the Chiên 
Đàn temples are less refined, with forms much 
thicker than those of early dancing figures, but 
still echoing the imagery from the sophisticated 
Trà Kiệu pedestal.

elevated pedestal carrying a sword in his left hand

throughout the relief to spread the visual ideals 
of courtly culture with the inclusion of celestial 
dancers and courtiers, a scene first carved on the 
Trà Kiệu pedestal.

Scheurleer 2011 : 113). There are variations for the 
placement of the arms in this special gesture, which 
includes the second hand clasping the elbow or the

conclusion
The 10th-century Trà Kiệu pedestal paired with a 
large sculptural liṅga-yoni installed on the top is a 
modern curatorial arrangement. The liṅga-yoni has 
little connection to the imagery carved on the Trà 
Kiệu pedestal, and may be dated earlier than the 
pedestal. Based on the carved images, I argue that 
the liṅga-yoni was unlikely to have been originally 
paired with the pedestal. Inscriptional evidence 
indicate that the R āmāyaṇa was wel l known in 
Campā and illustrated on the foundation reliefs of 
the 10th-century Khương Mỹ temples. This chapter 
has moved the study of the pedestal beyond the 
issue of dating and identification, and connected 
the object to a larger corpus of Cam, Khmer, and 
Javanese art in the 9th–10 th centuries, as well as 
later Javanese art found in Candi Panataran.
The imagery of the Trà Kiệu pedestal documents 
the artistic exchange of Java and Khmer culture 
in the 9th–10 th centuries. There are three icono-
graphic elements—archers with bows, architectural 
features, and dancing apsaras es—that I interpret 
as reinforcing courtly culture, which scholars have 
shown to have some Sinitic links. The Trà Kiệu 
pedestal presents for the first time in Cam art 
carved images reflecting battle and hunting scenes, 
which foreshadow the growing number of images 
related to combat scenes with bows and arrows, 
horse-chariots, and warriors. The 11 th-century 
foundation bases at the Chiên Đàn temples and 
reliefs from Chánh Lộ and Mỹ Sơn also echo the 
imagery on the Trà Kiệu pedestal. Through the 10 th 
and 11th centuries, one notes an increased artis -
tic production of hunting and royal scenes, which 
were not religious, but rather reflected the courtly 
culture of Campā.
The images reveal attention to military expan-
sion, courtly kingship, and artistic alliance among 
the independent entities of Campā, alongside other 
contemporary cultures in the regions of Cambo -dia and Java. Offering an alternative reading of 
the Trà Kiệu pedestal, I suggest that it was not in-
tended to be the mount for a liṅga-yoni veneration 
in altar-pedestal form—the pīṭha of Śiva. Rather, 
the pedestal represents a colossal monument in 
itself, commemorating royal-divine characters in 
a temple context with secular and sacred mean -
ings. In conjunction with highlighting royal and 
sacred relationships with Viṣṇu in the Rāmāyaṇa, 
the t
extual and visual evidence from Trà Kiệu and 
later Cam art emphasize a Cam courtly culture 
whose iconography indicates close relationships 
to that of Khmer, East Javanese, and Chinese 
culture. In the 9th–10 th centuries, influence from 
the South occurred in Campā, rather than being 
directly imported from India. It reflected a courtly 
and military ethos shared across the southern seas 
by Campā, Cambodia, Java, and China.

Chapter 10
On the Chronological Interrelationship between 
Newly Found Inscriptions and the Temple Architecture of Campā: 
The Hòa Lai and Po Dam Sites 
Trần Kỳ Phương
introduction
In recent years, there have been several impor-
tant new findings of Cam inscriptions. Dated 
inscriptions in particular have provided rele -
vant information about the contemporary temple 
groups on the basis of a comparison with their art 
styles. As Cam temple sites are rarely associated 
with dated inscriptions, these new findings help to 
clarify some issues related to the temples’ dating. 
The new dates suggested here for relevant instances 
of Cam temple architecture will also provide a 
new comprehension of the relationships between 
the art of the Cams and their neighbours, namely 
pre-Angkorian Cambodia and Central Java.
on art styles of cam temple sites 
Henri Parmentier was the first to list and classify 
Cam temple architecture in his classic two-volume 
book Inventaire descriptif des monuments čams  
de l’Annam, published in 1909  and 1918 . In his 
work, Parmentier (1918 : 19–20) categorized Cam 
architecture into six forms, as follows:
1.  ‘L’art primitif’: Mỹ Sơn A1 style, around the 
early 7th century, along with the Po Nagar 
Northwest  tower and the Po Nagar main 
tower (restored in 813  and 817  CE);
2.  ‘L’art cubique’: Hòa Lai style, around the 
early 8th century, along with Mỹ Sơn F1 
tower and Po Nagar West tower (third half 
of the 9th century);
3.  ‘L’art mixte’: Đồng Dương style, around the 
year 875 CE;4.  ‘L’art classique’: Tháp Bạc Tower style, 
around the 11 th century, along with Mỹ 
Sơn E4 tower;
5.  ‘L’art dérivé’: Po Kloong Garai style, around 
the 12th century, along with Mỹ Sơn B1 
(1114  CE), Mỹ Sơn G1 ( 1157  CE), Po Kloong 
Garai (early 14 th century), and Po Rome 
(second quarter of the 17 th century);
6.  ‘L’art pyramidal’: The style of Po Nagar Nha 
Trang South tower and Bằng An tower (900  
and 910 CE), Po Nagar South tower (1145  
CE), and Yang Prong tower (early 14 th 
century). 
Parmentier’s classic work has been the basis for 
all subsequent research works on Cam art. It was 
not until 1942  that the classification and arrange-
ment of Cam temples according to artistic styles 
was initiated by Philippe Stern in his work L’art 
du Champa et son évolution. In this work, Stern 
applied the method of analysing decorative fea-
tures of art works, known as ‘motif analysis’ or 
‘decorative pattern analysis’ (analyse de motif), as 
was proposed by French art historians in the 20 th 
century to study South Asian arts. That method 
has brought positive results to the dating of ar-
tistic works by analysing patterns/motifs in detail 
and comparing them with each other, defining 
and classifying them according to each style (art 
stylistics), and finally comparing the development 
of each style in relation to its historical chronology 
in order to discern the probable period of the as-
sociated architectural works (Williams 1982 : 6–7). 
Accordingly, Stern suggested the following relative 
chronology for the art styles of Cam temples:
10_CreSouthV1_7P_11Feb22.indd   334 11/2/22   3:53 PM

--- [Page 337] ---
Newly Found Inscriptions and the Temple Architecture of Campā335
1.  Ancient style, as in the Mỹ Sơn E1 temple
 
and pedestal. This is assumed to belong to 
the 8th century by comparison with Damrei 
Krap temple of Khmer art on the moun-
tain of Phnom Kulen in Siem Reap province, 
even though Stern was uncertain about the 
date of that site (Stern 1942 : 69);
2.  Hòa Lai style, as in the Hòa Lai group with 
three towers, which was built in the first half 
of the 9th century. This style is related to 
the art of the Damrei Krap Khmer temple, 
because that temple is related to a Khmer in -
scription that must have postdated the cor-
onation of King Jayavarman II on Phnom 
Kulen, which is traditionally ascribed to the 
year 802 CE. Stern also thought that the 
Damrei Krap brick temple was built by Cam 
artisans in Khmer territory (Stern 1942 : 63);
3.  Đồng Dương style, inheriting complex and 
twisted pattern motifs of the Hòa Lai style 
and developing into a unique motif of Cam 
art. This motif, which has a wormlike shape 
(vermiculé) with deep carving, was applied 
in the decoration of temple architecture as 
well as sculpture during this art period. This 
style is related to the inscription of King 
Indravarman II erected at the Buddhist 
monastery in situ in 875  CE. Accordingly, 
the chronological frame of the Đ ồng Dương 
style can be attributed to the period from 
the second half of the 9th century to the first 
quarter of the 10 th century; 
4.  Mỹ Sơn A1 style: a major style, beginning
 
with the Khương Mỹ group of three towers. 
Stern highlighted the pattern motifs influ-
enced by Khmer and Javanese arts in this 
tower group, and the direct succession of the 
pattern units from the ‘vermicular pattern’ 
of the Đồng Dương style in Khương Mỹ. He 
proposed to date the Khương Mỹ group to 
shortly before 920  CE, which would also 
coincide with the starting point of Mỹ Sơn 
A1 style. In the Mỹ Sơn A1 style, a common 
architectural decoration was foliage pattern 
units with an uninterrupted S-shaped layout, 
which created airy and gentle beauty, quite 
differently from the typical ‘vermicular 
pattern’ of the Đ ồng Dương style;5.  Transition style between the Mỹ Sơn A1 
and Bình Định styles, following a historical 
event related to the transfer of the capital 
of Campā  from Quảng Nam to Bình Định 
around the year 1000  CE. Stern suggest-
ed that this style began in the early 11 th 
century;
6.  Bình Định style, defined on the basis of 
the relationship between Cam and Khmer 
arts. Stern suggested that the date of the 
Dương Long group of three towers and the 
Hưng Thạnh tower (Twin Towers) was in 
the late 12 th century or early 13 th century. 
He pointed out the profound influence of 
Khmer decorative art on those two tower 
groups, which he thought were influenced 
by Angkor Wat. Stern also proposed a 12 th 
century dating for the other tower groups 
in Bình Định province, such as Cánh Tiên, 
Thủ Thiện, and Thố c Lốc. According to him, 
most of the towers of the transitional period 
were dateable to the 11 th century, for in-
stance, the Bình Lâm tower in the early 11 th 
century and the tower group of Tháp Bạc in 
the late 11 th century;
7.  Late style. Stern proposed a date between 
the late 13 th century and the early 14 th 
century for the Po Kloong Garai temple, and 
the 17th century for the Po Rome temple. 
The above style and date classification table sug -
gested by Stern has been widely used in research 
works related to the history of Cam and other 
Southeast Asian arts.1 In the 1990 s, with funding 
from the Toyota Foundation, together with Shige-
eda Yutaka, I systematically carried out research on 
the Cam temple architecture in Central Vietnam. 
The research results were published in a catalogue 
entitled Champa Oukoku no iseki to bunka (‘Ruins 
1. For example, the study of Cam sculpture La statu -
aire du Champa  by Jean Boisselier, published in 1963, is 
mainly based on Stern’s classification of art style, although 
Boisselier supplemented the division with shorter periods 
within each style and slightly modified some of the dates. 
Stern’s classification of art style has widely been applied 
by Vietnamese researchers in their works, such as Tr ần Kỳ 
Phương  (1988), Ngô Văn Doanh (1994), and Nguyễn H ồng 
Kiên (2000).

Trần Kỳ Phương336
and Culture of the Kingdom of Campā ’) on the 
occasion of Cam art exhibition to commemo -
rate the 20 th anniversary of The Toyota Founda-
tion, 1974 –1994 , in Tokyo in 1994  (Shigeeda and 
Momoki 1994 ); and in a co-authored work entitled 
Champa iseki: Umi ni mukatte tatsu  (‘Cam ruins: 
Standing toward the Ocean’) published in Japan in 
1997  (Trần Kỳ Phương ad Shigeeda 1997 ).
In these works, Shigeeda set up a table com -
paring the ground plans of Cam temples in each 
style on the basis of the drawings by Parmenti -
er. This comparison shows the differences and 
similarities of each Cam architectural group for 
each building and style (Shigeeda and Momoki 
1994). Shigeeda also proposed a different means 
of architectural classification for Cam art in each 
complex on the basis of research conducted on 
the following Cam temple structures (Shigeeda 
and Momoki 1994: 9–64):
1.  Mỹ Sơn complex: including the temple 
groups of Mỹ Sơn site, the dates range 
from the 7 th to the 13 th or 14 th centuries. 
The complex represents the process of Cam 
temple architecture from the early to the late 
periods in terms of architectural concept, 
structural technique, and decorative pro-
grammes and patterns;
2.  Quảng Nam complex: including the temple 
groups in Quảng Nam province, such as 
Đồng Dương, Khương Mỹ, Chiên Đàn, and 
Bằng An, the dates range from the late 9th 
to the 13th centuries. The complex includes 
various art styles and architectural forms of 
Buddhist and Brahmanical temples;
3.  Bình Định complex: including the temple 
groups in Bình Định province, such as Bình 
Lâm, Tháp Bạc (Silver tower), Dương Long, 
Hưng Thạnh, Cá nh Tiên, Thủ Thiện, Thố c 
Lốc, and Tháp Nhạn, in Tuy Hòa city, Phú 
Yên province, the dates range from the 11 th 
to the 13 th centuries. The complex repre-
sents the full development of Cam temple 
architecture in terms of the trans-regional 
art exchanges in m ainland Southeast Asia;
4.  Po Nagar complex: including the temples at 
the Po Nagar Nha Trang site in Nha Trang city, Khánh Hòa province, the dates range 
from the 8th to the 13 th centuries. The 
complex represents the art mixture between 
the North and South Campā;
5.  Phú Hài complex: including the temple 
groups of Phú Hài, Po Dam and Hòa Lai 
in Bình Thuận and Ninh Thuận provinc-
es, the dates range from the 8th to the 9th 
centuries. The complex represents the early 
temple groups, which clearly displays the 
features of temple architecture within the 
same art period; 
6.  Po Kloong Garai complex: including the 
temple groups of Po Kloong Garai and Po 
Rome in Ninh Thuận province, the dates 
range from the 13 th to the 17 th centuries. 
The complex represents the features of Cam 
temple architecture of the late period. 
The development of Cam construction techniques 
is clearly shown in the six temple complexes listed 
above and also reveals features of each art style in 
every complex, which are influenced by, and syn-
cretized to, each other. The classification of Shige-
eda shows a process of gradual development of 
Cam temple construction techniques, which were 
clearly manifested in each complex, and also in -
dicates an interactive influence between art styles 
and regional architecture. For the dating of each 
site, Shigeeda basically applied Stern’s chrono -
logical table, though he supplemented and mod-
ified it on the basis of  his findings on the temple 
structural techniques implemented at each site. 
Since, in many cases, the sites have passed through 
phases of restoration, one cannot uniquely rely on 
the method of analysing pattern motif (analyse de 
motif) on those vestiges.
Therefore, to study Cam temple architecture we 
can fruitfully apply both classifications, i.e. Stern’s 
‘art style’ and Shigeeda’s ‘temple complex’, which 
complement each other. By approaching the minor 
architectural details of construction techniques 
along with decorative programmes and/or orna -
mented pattern units, and then by analysing and 
comparing them according to certain correlations 
existing among the monuments, we can try to find 
a solution for the relative date of a given temple.

the new findings of cam dated 
inscriptions and their relationship 
with temple architecture 
Over the years, many archaeological excavations 
have been carried out for restoration purposes at 
the sites of Hòa Lai, Po Dam, Tháp Bạc, Bình Lâm, 
Dương Long, Khương Mỹ, and Chiên Đàn. These 
excavations have unearthed many sandstone sculp-
tural works and some dated inscriptions. Most of 
these inscriptions, either in Sanskrit or Old Cam, 
have been translated into English and French by 
Arlo Griffiths and his colleagues in the context of 
the project ‘Corpus of Cam Inscriptions’ of the 
École française d’Extrême-Orient in Paris.2 In this 
chapter I present some dated inscriptions discov-
ered at the temple sites of Hòa Lai and Po Dam. I 
will compare the date provided in the inscriptions

(last accessed 6 May 2018). with the coterminous temples and analyse their 
artistic features, especially those that are specific and typical, and then propose a possible date for 
each temple and style. In doing so, firstly I intro-
duce the main sacred architectural sites built in the 
Pāṇḍuraṅga region, including the Phú Hài group, 
for which the relationship between inscriptions 
and temples will be discussed (Fig. 10.1).

Thuận provinces. The lowland of the provinces is 
the driest area in Central Vietnam; however, it also 
owns the rich sources of fresh water. Historically, 
this land occupied the prosperous ports located

er 1918 : 566). According to Stern (1942 : 63), Phú 
Hài is probably mi-khmèr mi-cham (‘half-Khmer 
half-Cam’). Meanwhile, Michel Jacq-Hergoualc’h 
(2001 : 50–56) argues that the principal temple of 
the Phú Hài site has a close artistic relationship 
with the Wat Keo temple in the Chaiya district, 
Surat Thani province in Peninsular Thailand, for 
instance, with respect to its architectural form and 
decorative details.
During the early 1990 s, the Institute of Mon -
ument Conservation of Ministry of Culture and 
Cultural Department of Bình Thuận province 
had investigated and excavated the bases of these 
temples. Especially significant was the excavation 
conducted from November 1994  to January 1995 , 
in which archaeologists revealed several stages of 
brick structures built through different periods of 
time (Nguyễn Xuân Lý and Nguyễn Hồ ng Kiên 
1995 : 100–111) (Fig. 10.5 ).
The Phú Hài temple group, along with the  
Po Dam and Hòa Lai, were classified as ‘Phú  
Hài complex’ by Shigeeda and Momoki (1994: 
55–59), on the basis of their own typical features  
of ground plan design, decorative pattern, and 
structural technique (Trần Kỳ Phương and Shige-
eda 1997: 158–172).

was completely destroyed by bombs at the end of 
the Vietnam War in 1975 ; furthermore, the recent 
restorations resulted in a clumsy and confused 
copy of the original structures. Since the Hòa Lai 
group of three towers was first described in detail 
by Parmentier (1909 : 98–108) in the early 20 th 
century and developed throughout the century, 
we primarily have to rely on the description and 
photographs provided by that French scholar to 
study the art of this group of temples.
The Hòa Lai group played a significant role 
in the evolution of Cam art. On the basis of their 
architectural form, decorative programme, and 
type of pattern, Parmentier classified them as Art 
cubique; meanwhile, Stern called them Style de 
Hòa Lai. One also notes a difference between the 
two scholars about the dating of this group.
The remarkable features of the Hòa Lai group, 
particularly the Middle and North towers, are the 
stout and solid form, large pilaster, thick cornice, 
three double false-doors formed by two overlap -
ping layers—the inner big and the outer small—, 
two large arches (grande arcature) above, a long 
and narrow vestibule, and the square ground 
layout. The decorative programme of the Middle 
and North towers is expressed with a linking 
design style of similar twisted, thick, and sinuous 
units of pattern; this is a distinctive and unique 
type, which is easy to contrast with other types of 
patterns in the Cam architectural decorative rep-
ertoire. Another remarkable feature of the Middle 
and North towers is that there are sixteen brick 
Garuḍa holy birds on the cornices. In the Hòa Lai 
group, sandstone corner ornaments (pièce d’accent 
en grès), which are a common decorative feature 
in Cam architecture from the Đ ồng Dương period 
onwards, have not appeared yet.
Parmentier’s classification of the South and 
Middle towers as ‘cubic art’ perhaps originated 
from the impression created by the structure of 
the tower: the upper part of the tower body is often 
figured to be a bigger tower-base to support the 
roof layers of the tower formed into overlapped 
cubes. Parmentier dated the Hòa Lai group to 
about the 8th–9 th century (1918 : 19–22, 536–40). 
His estimate was based on the comparison with 
other Cam ruins linked to epitaphs (1918 : 1–4). 
Although Parmentier’s approach was later criti-cized and replaced by a new approach proposed 
by Stern (1942 : 92–98), the date he suggested  for 
the Hòa Lai group is still valid.4
As I mentioned above, when rethinking Cam 
art history, Stern (1942 : 4, 8–9, and 47 –48) chose a 
specific monument to identify each typical artistic 
period; thus, he replaced the expression ‘cubic art’ 
of Parmentier with ‘Hòa Lai style’. Stern agreed 
with Parmentier that each of the Hòa Lai towers 
was built separately, the South tower having been 
possibly built the earliest and its architectural 
form and technical structure being followed by 
the Middle tower and then the North tower, and 
he proposed a date between the middle of the 8th 
century and the first half of the 9 th century (1942 : 
61–62). Remarkably, Stern assumed a similarity 
between the Hòa Lai group and Damrei Krap 
temple on Phnom Kulen mountain in Cambodia.5

On the basis of a detailed study of that temple, 
he noticed its similarities to Cam architecture, 
especially to the Hòa Lai group. Relying on his 
reference about the date of Damrei Krap temple, 
which was fairly later than the enthronement of 
King Jayavarman II on Phnom Kulen, tradition -
ally ascribed to the year 802  CE, he estimated that 
the Hòa Lai site was built slightly later than the 
Damrei Krap temple, and came to the conclusion 
that the temple must date from the first half of the 
9th century (Stern 1942 : 63). However, I maintain 
that Stern exaggerated the connections between 
Prasat Damrei Krap and the Hò a Lai temples and 
that whatever the exact date of Damrei Krap may 
be, that date has no bearing on the dating of the 
Hòa Lai temples.
Later, in his research work on Cam sculpture, 
Boisselier accepted Stern’s opinion that the three 
towers of the Hòa Lai group were built later than 
Damrei Krap temple in Cambodia, as well as Par-
mentier’s conclusions about their successive build -
ing stages. However, he claimed that the date of 
Damrei Krap temple was a little later, in the second 
quarter of the 9 th century; and the date he pro -
posed for Hòa Lai temples was also in accordance 
with previous proposals, namely the third quarter 
of the 9 th century (Boisselier 1963 : 84). 
We now return to Stern’s analysis of the Hòa Lai 
group’s architectural and decorative programmes 
after which he named the ‘Hòa Lai style’ in the 
history of Cam art. As in the other styles, Stern 
mainly relied on the analysis of pattern design 
displayed on large arches (grande arcature) and 
Authority at the temple of East Mebon in Siem Reap in 
July 2015). For this reason, Stern suggested that the brick 
architectural elements of the temple were built by Cam 
artisans, while the stone parts by Khmer artisans. In fact, 
upon detailed comparison, the Damrei Krap temple is not 
similar to the temples of Hòa Lai group. For example, the 
brick decorative Garuḍa birds on the cornices, the design 
of pillars, the false doors, the tympanums as well as the 
structure of the upper parts are features that differentiate 
the two temple complexes from each other. Furthermore, 
there are various Khmer brick temples that are coterminous 
with the Damrei Krap temple on Phnom Kulen, which 
suggests that this temple was not necessarily built by Cam 
architects. Be this as it may, both temple groups were built 
on the basis of a common temple architectural scheme 
found in the entire Southeast Asian region at that time. big pilasters to characterize each artistic style. In 
the Hòa Lai group, he mainly took interest in the 
Middle and North towers, whose decorative pro-
grammes were richer than the South tower, which, 
he remarked, presented some curious and original 
aspects (Stern 1942 : 15). The type of decorative 
pattern to which Stern referred is characterized 
by units appearing in twisted, thin, and sinuous 
shapes, intentionally repeated to create a rhythm 
of decoration for the prominent features of the 
temple, such as large arches and pilasters. The 
large arches above the double false doors of the 
Middle and North towers are unique because they 
are formed by two overlapping blocks, the inner 
high and the outer low. This is a type of unique 
‘double arch’ arranged with similar linking pattern 
units, which do not appear in other styles. As for 
the pillars, these uninterrupted pattern units are 
only expressed in the middle part and not on both 
sides to create an airy beauty for the walls without 
any overuse of decoration patterns. This style is 
completely different from that of the temples of 
Đồng Dương.
In 2006, while carrying out restoration work, 
the Ninh Thuận Provincial Museum discovered a 
92 cm-high stele together with its base at the Hòa 
Lai group, in between the Middle and North towers. 
This important inscribed stele was translated and 
published by Griffiths and Southworth (2011). The 
Hòa Lai stele, dating back to the year 700 Śaka (778 
CE), provides the main text of the Sanskrit inscrip-
tion; its base, 25.5 cm high, which was carved with 
two lines of poetry (śloka), bears a later date, i.e. 760 
Śaka (838/839 CE). These two different dates are 
closely related to the period in which the Hòa Lai 
temple group was built (Southworth 2012: 68–70). 
The stele mentioned the dominance of Śaiva beliefs, 
the matrilineal ideology in inheritance, and the 
local tradition of producing Sanskrit stelae initiat-
ed under the reign of Satyavarman, the great king 
who erected important stelae in Pāṇḍuraṅga and 
was praised by his successors in the inscriptions 
found at the Cam royal sanctuary of Po Nagar in 
Nha Trang, formerly Kauṭhāra state (Griffiths and 
Southworth 2011: 17).

the two dates (778  and 838 /839 CE) of the stele as

well as of the stele’s base and the Hòa Lai temples,

probable construction date for each building. If 
the three temples of the Hòa Lai group were built 
at three different times, which temple was corre-
sponding to the date of the stele and the stele’s 
base? To answer this question, we must examine 
and compare the order of construction of each 
temple, so as to be able to advance an appropriate 
date for each corresponding construction work.
Judging from the construction technique, ar -
chitectural form, and decorative programmes, as 
shown by previous authors, the South tower is 
considered to have been built the earliest, fol -
lowed by the Middle tower and finally the North 
tower. We see that the structure of the South tower 
is short and big, whereas the temple base (sou -
bassement) is high; the double false door is huge 
and thick with two layers, the inner bigger than 
the outer, on which two rectangular frames with 
dual contours were carved. There is no decorative pattern whatsoever on the large arches and the 
tower walls. Notably, on both sides of each false 
door two miniature towers without details were 
carved; these miniature towers form a decorative 
motif known as ‘flying palace’, which was com -
monly sculpted on the Khmer brick temples of 
Sambor Prei Kuk, dated to the 7 th–8 th centuries 
(Nakagawa and Shimoda 2003 : 120, 229; Tranet 
1997 : 239–253) (Fig. 10.7). In Cam architecture, the 
motif of the ‘flying palace’ only appeared in the 
South tower of the Hòa Lai sanctuary; therefore, 
it is the only evidence we have to compare with 
the neighbou ring arts, especially Khmer art of the 
8th century. In the light of the more simplified 
ground plan structure and programme as well 
as the simpler architectural and decorative pro -
gramme of the South tower in comparison to the 
other two towers, researchers agree that the South 
tower is the earliest temple of the Hòa Lai group 
(Parmentier 1918 : 32; Stern 1942 : 910; Boisselier 
1963 : 84; Shigeeda and Momoki 1994 : 57, 97–98; 
Trần Kỳ Phương and Shigeeda 1997 : 170–171).

Due to the complete destruction of the Middle 
tower during the war, I did not have the opportu-
nity to carry out research in situ, but could only 
approach the site through the works of previous 
scholars. As mentioned above, Parmentier assert-
ed that the Middle tower was built after the South 
tower. The salient feature of the Middle tower is its 
double false doors with large arches decorated with 
the thick and sinuous patterns described above, and especially the image of dvārapālas (temple 
guardians/door tutelary deities) standing inside 
the false doors above the temple base. This is the 
first appearance of this motif in Cam temple archi -
tecture. Another architectural decorative feature 
of the Middle tower is the feet of pilasters deco -
rated with small arches whose centre features a 
kīrtimukha/kāla figure and two patterns of ribbons 
dropping down from both sides. This motif reveals 
an artistic relationship between Central Java and 
Campā (Baptiste 2014 : 72–73). Under the small 
arch there are human images standing on the 
arc-shaped or star-shaped (flower?) patterns 
(Fig. 10.8). That feature can be compared with the 
small arches on the facade of Mỹ Sơn E1 pedes -
tal, showing a stylistic continuity between the two 
artworks (Stern 1942 : 15–16). In comparing the 
Middle tower and the South tower, we can see that 
the ground-plan layout as well as the architectur-
al decoration of the Middle tower is much more 
complex and sophisticated than the South tower. 
All these features indicate that it must have been 
built later than the South tower.
According to Boisselier, two dvārapāla bas-re-
liefs carved on two false doors of the Middle tower 
(Fig. 10.9) evoke a similarity with the dvārapā -
la bas-reliefs of the Chót Mạt tower of Khmer 
pre-Angkorian art period built in Tây Ninh prov-
ince, Vietnam, as well as the human figures of 
Candi Bhīma on Dieng Plateau in Central Java, In -
donesia. Boisselier also analysed and compared the 
dvārapālas’ sampot with loose broad flaps falling 
to the knees, its spiral hair, and its round earrings 
with some sculptural works of Mỹ Sơn, such as the 
hair and clothing of the demon king Rāvaṇa on the 
tympanum of Mỹ Sơn F1 temple or of the dancing 
Śiva represented on the tympanum of Mỹ Sơn C1 
temple, and the sampot of the standing Gaṇeśa 
statue of Mỹ Sơn E5 . Then, Boisselier (1963 : 84–85) 
asserted that the two dvārapāla bas-reliefs of the 
Middle tower belonged to the extended period of Mỹ Sơn E1 style, dating to about the third quarter 
of the 9th century—being almost contemporary in 
period with the Đ ồng Dương style, which began 
around 875 CE.

ground- plan layout of the group, and its decora-

4.  The Middle tower shows the close relation-
ship with neighbou ring sites, such as those 
of Cambodia (Stern 1942 : 63–64; Boisseli -
er 1963 : 84–85), Java (Baptiste 2014 : 72–73; 
Griffiths 2014 : 297), and Southern Thailand 
or Peninsular Malaysia (Jacq-Hergoualc’h 
2001 : 50–56). This reflects a contemporane-
ous cultural interaction in the whole region 
through trading connections by land and 
waterways (Trầ n Kỳ Phương 2013 : 47–51; 
2017 : 4–6).
Based on the content of the Hòa Lai stele, Griffiths 
and Southworth (2011 : 296) reasoned that the god 
mentioned in the text, Ādideveśvara, who was as-
sociated with goddess Durgā, was worshipped in 
the Middle tower; and that this stele was erected 
to commemorate the groundbreaking ceremony 
or the inauguration of this temple. Therefore, the 
important information provided by the Hòa Lai 
stele about the religious activities under the con-
temporary reign of King Satyavarman falls within 
the period of Cam temple architecture that the 
Middle tower typically exemplifies. Moreover, 
Baptiste (2014 : 73, fig. 64 ) connected the date of 
the Hòa Lai stele (778  CE) with the Middle tower 
by analysing the influence of Javanese art, espe-
cially the Kāla image, in the decorative patterns 
of this temple. Thus, it can be safely assumed that 
the date of 778  CE is likely to fall within the range 
of the construction period of the Middle tower.
If 778 CE is considered as contemporaneous 
to the period of construction of the Middle tower, 
then the North tower is likely to be attributed 
to 838/839 CE—the date inscribed on the base of 
the Hòa Lai stele: as argued by Stern, this tower 
belonged to the latest stage of the Hòa Lai style 
(1942 : 91). Thus, the Middle tower may have been 
built by King Satyavarman in 778 CE, as described 
in his stele; later, during the reconstruction of the 
North tower, King Vikrāntavarman had a new ste -
le-base made in 838 /839 CE to support the original 
stele erected by King Satyavarman (Griffiths and 
Southworth 2011 : 295, 301).7
Interestingly, the period of sixty years sepa-
rating these two dates shows us the full process

Po Dam Group (Fig. 10.12)
The Po Dam temple complex is located in the 
Tuy Tịnh commune, Tuy Phong district, Bình 
Thuận province, at a distance of approx. 60  km 
from the Hoa Lai temple group. It consists of 
six architectural works named by Parmentier as 
follows: (1 ) Central tower, (2 ) Northeast tower, (3) 
Northwest tower, (4 ) South tower, (5 ) Southeast 
tower, and (6 ) Southwest tower. The Northeast 
and Northwest towers were completely destroyed 
(Parmentier 1909 : 50–58; Stern 1942 : 15–16; Trầ n 
Kỳ Phương and Shigeeda 1997 : 158–161). Po Dam 
is the only temple complex known in Cam archi-
tecture whose axis is oriented to the southwest. 
The axis of this tower group is likely to relate to 
the location and layout of a temple complex built 
on a narrow area of a low hill next to the mountain 
slope; however, it could possibly reflect specific 
features of Cam beliefs.8 
8. The direction of the main gate of Cam temples ( kalan ) 
did not always resemble the Indian prototype, i.e. facing 
east, but depended on the terrain where the temple was 
built. In Mỹ Sơn, for example, the temple-towers were 
built in a valley symbolizing a maṇḍala ; thus, the main 
gate of the kalan  opens out to both the eastern and western 
directions, similar to those of the temples in Central Java in 
the early period (Klokke 1994: 76–77). In the case of the Po 
Dam group, the southern direction slanting to the west is an 
ideal direction for the main gate of a kalan , because it faces 
a vast field ahead; moreover, as the sea-coast in this region 
slants to the south, then the temple could be regarded as 
facing the sea. In addition, the Po Dam group possibly had a 
close relationship with the Phú Hài group if it is considered 
in the light of the Cam concept of dichotomous universe. 
This includes such opposites as male–female, mountain–
sea, father–mother, areca–coconut, and so on ( Trần Kỳ 
Phương and Nakamura 2012: 274– 275). Accordingly, the 
Po Dam group is likely to belong to the mountain-father 
dichotomy; meanwhile, the Phú Hài group belongs to the 
sea-mother dichotomy.

In general, the Po Dam group displays the 
architectural form that was popular in the early 
period of Cam temples. This is expressed by the 
low size of the towers, the narrow interiors, and 
the small square ground plans with short vesti -
bules. The Po Dam temples were built successively 
within a short period of time—perhaps only a few 
decades. The Cam temples that are similar to this 
kind of architectural type include the small tower 
of Phú Hài, Mỹ Sơn C7 ( Trần Kỳ Phương 1988 : 
36–37), and the Mỹ Khánh tower.9
In terms of architectural form, ground plan, 
and decorative programme, as well as the cor -
belling in the interiors, we can see that the South, 
Southeast and Southwest towers of the Po Dam 
group (Fig. 10.13 ) were built the earliest because 
the decorative programmes on the walls of these 
towers are simple, with a big pilaster without dec-
orative pattern in the middle. There is no false 
door and arch, and the cornice is formed with 
straight edges. Also, a comparison can be carried 
out between the corbelling in the interior of the 
Southeast tower and the small tower of Phú Hài.

closed by a square block of stone, now lost, similar
