small temple, with an east-facing door, was entirely built 
of brick, without any trace of stone. There were only brick 
walls, without corbelling. The roof of the temple was pos -
sibly covered with light material (thatch, wood, or tile) as 
archaeologists have not found any traces of stone materials 
around the tower. Its three false doors are decorated with 
big arches without any patterns, and there are standing 
human images, very roughly carved, inside the false doors. 
Radiocarbon dating (C14) yields a date of 750 ± 40 CE 
for the Mỹ Khánh tower (Trịnh Nam Hải 2001: 81). The 
architectural form of the Mỹ Khánh tower is quite similar 
to the South, Southeast, and Southwest towers of the Po 
Dam group, especially the detail of curved edges of the 
two walls connecting with the main hall of the Southwest tower. This reflects the earliest period of Cam temple ar -
chitecture, characterized by a simple structural technique 
and simplified decorative program me, a low small shape, 
and a narrow interior ( Trần Kỳ Phương 2011: 288– 291). The 
radiocarbon dating of Mỹ Khánh tower mentioned above 
is a valuable reference in comparison with the date of the inscription newly found in the Po Dam group, i.e. 710 CE.to the one of the small tower of Phú Hài (Fig. 10.4) 
(Trần Kỳ Phương 2011 : 292). It can also be com-
pared with a minor detail in the vestibule of the 
Southwest tower and the Mỹ Khánh tower, i.e. two 
corners of the wall along the entrance to the ves-
tibule, which connect with the sanctum of these two towers, and which were sharpened into two 
curved edges. From this detail it may be inferred 
that they were possibly built simultaneously. That 
unique feature also appears  in the small temple of 
Mỹ Sơn C7 , the North tower of the Phú Hài group, 
and in the Middle tower of the Hòa Lai group.10 
This is a significant feature of Cam temple archi-
tecture during the early period (Trầ n Kỳ Phương 
2011 : 288–289).
The Central tower of the Po Dam group  
(Fig. 10.14 ) belongs to a more highly developed 
stage of construction technique and architectur -
al decoration, as manifested in the rectangular 
ground plan with long vestibule. It is the largest 
sized temple and was built the latest among the 
other towers of the group. A series of three single 
false-doors expressing the big arch (grande arca-
ture) appear in this temple;11 two of them having 
been lost, only the big arch of the western false door 
remains. The layout of the decorative programme  
on the big arch on the western false door of the 
Central tower includes thick and sinuous pattern 
units hanging down with four circular flowers 
overlapping both sides of the pilaster at the end; 
the contour on the top of the pilaster is adorned 
with two double 8-shaped pattern units linking a 
double rectangular frame. Especially important is 
a unique pattern on the eastern cornice of the ves-
tibule expressing a kīrtimukha/kāla figure, which 
10. The two edges of the walls connecting the vestibule 
with the sanctum were curved, possibly in order to create a 
convenient entrance to the sanctum because of the narrow 
vestibule. Further references on this feature can be found 
in the plan drawings made by Parmentier (1909: Planches I, 
VI, XVI, LXXXIV) of the North tower of the Phú Hài group, 
the Southwest tower of the Po Dam group, the Middle tower 
of the Hòa Lai group, and the Mỹ Sơn C7 tower.
11. Single arches with only one layer were placed on 
single false doors; meanwhile, double arches were placed 
on double false doors at the Hòa Lai group. This type of 
double arches gave the temple a solid and stout beauty, cre -
ating the impression of a stronger and more imposing form.

the Śaka year marked by (1 ) Earth, (3 ) Fires, (6)

If so, which tower of the Po Dam group corre-
sponds to the date inscribed on the slab-stone? Ac-
cording to the analysis presented above, the date of 
the Central tower of the Po Dam group is possibly 
contemporary with the Middle tower of the Hòa 
Lai group, that is around the year 778  mentioned 
in the Hòa Lai stele; therefore, the year 710  CE of 
the Po Dam inscription is not appropriate for the 
Central tower. Accordingly, the year 710  CE can 
only be matched with the South, Southeast, and 
Southwest towers, which are works belonging to 
the early period, characterized by a simple struc-
tural style as analysed above. Thus, I suggest that 
the date 710 CE mentioned in the Po Dam inscrip-
tion is closely related to the early temple group 
of this site, including the South, Southeast, and 
Southwest towers, mainly because the period from 
710 to 778  CE, lasting around seventy years, can 
be regarded as the necessary duration to advance 
the techniques of brick temple construction that 
started in the early stage of Cam architecture. The 
development of the temple structures can clearly 
be seen from the simpler and smaller works of 
the Phú Hài group or of the South, Southeast, and 
Southwest towers of the Po Dam group (Figs. 10.3 
15. Arlo Griffiths, email dated 12 February 2015. and 10.13 ),16 as well as of the South tower of the 
Hòa Lai group. This development goes from sim-
plistic decorative programmes to the larger and 
more sophisticated Central tower of the Po Dam 
group, or of the Middle tower as well as the North 
tower of the Hòa Lai group. This exemplifies the 
course of the development of Cam temple archi-
tecture in the Southern region of the Cam king -
dom(s) during the 8 th and 9 th centuries.
conclusion

Hòa Lai and Po Dam makes an important contri-

16. In 2013 and 2014, archaeological excavations were 
conducted at Po Dam by the Center for Archaeological 
Research, Southern Institute of Social Sciences in Ho 
Chi Minh City and Bình Thuận Provincial Museum. The 
result of the two excavations unearthed the remains of 
previous brick buildings including several smaller shrines, 
maṇḍapa s, gopura s, stairways, and so on (Fig. 10.17). Ac -

tions, archaeologists revealed that the base of the Southern 
tower was built as overlapping the bases of the Southeastern 
and Southwestern towers. Thus, one can argue that the 
Southern tower was built at a slightly later period than 
the Southeastern and Southwestern ones (Nguyễn Khánh 
Trung Kiên and Nguyễn Xuân Lý 2016: 730–731; Nguyễn

Cam art history. These documents provide com -
pelling evidence, complementing new perceptions 
on the dating of Cam temples in the context of two 
architectural classifications, the ‘art style’ classi -
fication of Stern and the ‘complex architecture’ 
classification of Shigeeda. These inscriptions help 
us to determine the appropriate date of the two 
temple groups of Hòa Lai and Po Dam, and further 
explore the development of each architectural 
complex by comparing them with such neigh-bouring arts as those of pre-Angkorian Cambodia 
and Central Java (Stern 1942 : 63–64; Baptiste 2014 : 
72–73; Griffiths 2014 : 57). On that basis, a general 
chronological framework, in which these artis -
tic developments had interactive influences, can 
be proposed to establish the correlation between 
art and architecture and the religious and socio-  
political background of Campā and its neighbour -
ing regions in Southeast Asia.

Andrea Acri (PhD, Leiden University) is Maî-
tre de conférences/Assistant Professor in Tantric Studies at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (EPHE, PSL University) in Paris. Prior to joining the EPHE in 2016 , he has held various research 
and teaching positions in India, Singapore, Aus-tralia, and the Netherlands. He is a member of the editorial board of the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society and the Journal of Yoga Studies. His main research and teaching interests are Śaiva and Buddhist tantric traditions, Hinduism and Indi-an Philosophy, Yoga studies, Sanskrit and Old Ja-vanese philology, and the comparative religious history of South and Southeast Asia from the pre-modern to the contemporary period. His publi-cations include the monograph Dharma Pātañ-jala (Egbert Forsten/Brill 2011 ; Aditya Prakashan 
2017 ; Indonesian translation EFEO/Gramedia 
2018 ), as well as various edited volumes and arti-
cles in international academic journals.
Mya Chau (PhD, University of California, Los 
Angeles) currently teaches at Loyola Marymount University and Chapman University. In addition, she serves as a Research Assistant for the Schol-ars Program and Curatorial Department at the Getty Research Institute. Her research examines Buddhist visual culture and artistic exchanges in India and Southeast Asia. In 2015 , she was a 
Blakemore Freeman Fellow and recipient of the 2019  Women of Vision Award.
Swati Chemburkar is an architectural histo-rian whose work focuses on Southeast Asia, es-pecially Cambodia. She directs a postgraduate diploma course on Southeast Asian Art and Ar-chitecture at Jnanapravaha, Mumbai. Her main research interests are Khmer architecture of the Bayon period and Hindu-Buddhist Tantra tra-ditions of Cambodia. Her recent publications include ‘Pāśupata Sect in Ancient Cambodia and Champa’ (2017 ) with Shivani Kapoor; ‘Stupa to 
Mandala: Tracing a Buddhist Architectural De-velopment from Kesariya, Borobudur to Tabo’ (2018 ); and ‘Khmer Empire and Southeast Asia 
(8th to 14 th centuries)’ (2018 ).
Olivier Cunin is a qualified architect with a doctorate in architecture (2004 ). Since 1999 , he 
has been researching in situ the Bayon-style mon-uments (late 12 th century–early 13 th century) 
and other Khmer constructions by applying the methods of building archaeology, scientific tech-niques of archaeometry, and graphic computer technic. He has contributed to three books on the most emblematic monuments of the Bayon style: Banteay Chhmar (2005 ), the Bayon temple 
(2007 ), and the Preah Khan of Angkor (2011 ). He 
was a consultant for several international teams working at Angkor, such as the Swiss Conser-vation Project at Banteay Srei (2008 ), the World 
Monuments Fund at Angkor Wat (2012 –2014 ), 
the International Cooperation Team of the Korea Cultural Heritage Foundation at the Preah Pithu temples group (2017 ) and since 2019  to the AP-
SARA authority and the French Embassy at the West Mebon temple.

 (PhD, UC Berkeley) is Professor of 
Indian and Southeast Asian Art at Harvard Uni-versity. Her research and teaching interests cover a broad range of topics, such as text-image rela-tionships, female representations and patronage, re-appropriation of sacred objects, and post-colo-nial discourse in the field of South and Southeast Asian Art. Her books include Receptacle of the Sacred: Illustrated Manuscripts and the Buddhist book cult in South Asia (2013 ) and Garland of Vi-
sions: Color, Tantra and a Material History of In-dian Painting ( 2021 ). In addition to her academic 
research, she is developing a digital humanities project on colour, which will serve as an online portal and a searchable, open database for exist-ing and future research on pigments. She has also co-curated an exhibition on Nepalese Buddhist Ritual Art and co-edited its catalog, Dharma and Puṇya: Buddhist Ritual Art of Nepal ( 2019 ).
Mai Bùi Diệu Linh is a part-time faculty member in the Department of Religions and Cultures at Concordia University in Montréal, Québec, Can-ada. She is finishing her doctoral dissertation on religious identity and practices among the Cam Ahier communities in contemporary Vietnam. Her investigation of Cam Ahier contemporary religion builds upon her previous research on the religions of mediaeval Campā. With a foun-dation in studies that included the history and philosophy of Hinduism and Buddhism in South Asia, she expanded her research area to embrace Southeast Asia, particularly with regard to ques-tions of the historical transmission and adoption of Indian culture, religion, and art in the region. It was her deep interest in Hindu-Buddhist reli-gious art, iconography, and sculptures of medi-aeval Campā that led her to engage with contem-porary Cam communities as a means of gaining a more complete understanding of Cam religion over time and space.
Tr
ần Kỳ Phương  is a former curator of the 
Danang Museum of Cham Sculpture, Vietnam 
(1978– 1999); currently he is a Senior Research 
Fellow with the Vietnam Association of Archae-ologists. His main research interests focus on the arts of Campā Kingdom, especially temple ar-chitecture and sculpture, as well as cultural area studies in Central Vietnam. He has published several books and articles in Vietnamese, English, and Japanese, including: Mỹ Sơn in the History of Cham Art ( 1988); Vestiges of Champa Civili-
zation (2008); Champ
ā Iseki: Umi ni mukatte 
tasu [Champ ā Ruins: Standing facing toward the 
Ocean]  (co-authored with Shige-eda Yutaku, 
1997); The Cham of Vietnam: History, Society
 
and Art (co-edited with Bruce Lockhart, 2011); Vibrancy in Stone: Masterpieces from the Danang Museum of Cham Sculpture (co-edited with Võ V. Thắng and Peter D. Sharrock, 2018).   
Peter D. Sharrock
 researches the art history 
of the Angkorian Khmer Empire and the Eso-
teric Buddhist and Hindu art of Maritime Asia from AD 800 to 1400 . He lectures at the SOAS 
University of London (the School of Oriental and African Studies), where he is a Project Board member of the School’s growing Southeast Asian Academic Art Programme (SAAAP).

Iain Sinclair  (PhD, Monash University) is an 
Honorary Research Fellow at the University of 
Queensland School of Historical and Philosoph-ical Inquiry. He is concurrently a Lecturer and Researcher at Nan Tien Institute, Wollongong. He has been a Visiting Fellow at the Nalanda-Sri-wijaya Centre, ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, and a Käte Hamburger Kolleg Fellow at the Centre for Religious Studies, Ruhr University Bochum. He studies the history of religion and art history us-ing primary sources in classical Asian languages. His published research focuses on Buddhist tan-tra, Sanskrit manuscripts, Newar Buddhism and the Buddhism of the Malay Archipelago.
